nameStory: These tiny freshwater clams earned their common name because they're about the size of your pinky fingernail - usually less than half an inch across! The "striated" part refers to the fine ridges or lines that run across their shells, like tiny grooves you might see on a vinyl record.
description: The Striated Fingernailclam is a tiny freshwater bivalve that looks like a miniature version of the clams you might find at the beach. These little mollusks have two hinged shell halves that are typically yellowish-brown to gray in color. They're quite small, usually measuring only about 6-12 millimeters (roughly a quarter to half inch) across. Despite their small size, they're actually complete little ecosystems unto themselves, filtering water and living partly buried in muddy or sandy lake and stream bottoms.

idTips.label: Fine shell ridges
idTips.description: Look for delicate concentric ridges running across the shell surface that you can feel with your fingertip - they're more pronounced than on other fingernailclams and give the shell a distinctly grooved texture

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: About the size of a child's pinky fingernail, typically 6-12mm across - small enough to easily sit on a dime with room to spare

idTips.label: Rounded shell shape
idTips.description: Nearly circular when viewed from above, not obviously longer than wide like some other small clams - feels smooth and dome-like when you run your thumb over it

idTips.label: Yellowish-brown color
idTips.description: Shell ranges from pale yellow to brown, sometimes with a slightly translucent quality that makes it look almost amber-like in good light

idTips.label: Fragile feel
idTips.description: Shell feels thin and delicate between your fingers - much more fragile than larger clams and can crack easily with gentle pressure

habitat: Found in quiet freshwater environments throughout New England, particularly in the muddy or sandy bottoms of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. They prefer areas with some organic matter in the sediment and are often found in shallow water near shorelines where they can filter-feed on algae and tiny particles. Look for them in areas with cattails, water lilies, or other aquatic vegetation where the water moves gently.

seasonality.spring: As water temperatures warm, clams become more active and easier to spot in shallow areas. This is when they're most likely to be moving around on the surface of lake or pond sediments.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're actively filter-feeding. Look for them in warm, shallow water areas where you might spot their tiny siphons extending above the sediment surface.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to burrow deeper into sediments. Often found when turning over rocks or disturbing bottom sediments while looking for other aquatic life.
seasonality.winter: Buried deep in bottom sediments where they remain dormant under ice. Nearly impossible to find during this season unless you're doing serious sediment sampling.

funFact: Despite being tiny, these little clams are actually hermaphrodites that can live for several years and brood their babies inside their shells like underwater kangaroos - the young clams develop in a special pouch and are released as fully-formed miniature versions of their parents!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other fingernailclams, but the Striated Fingernailclam has more pronounced ridges on its shell that you can actually feel with your finger. Memory trick: "Striated = ridged like a scratched record" - if you can feel distinct grooves, it's likely this species rather than its smoother relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting they're related to marine clams, fingernailclams are actually more closely related to freshwater mussels. The "clam" name is a bit misleading - they're technically freshwater bivalve mollusks that have evolved separately from their ocean cousins.
compareHints: The Striated Fingernailclam differs from the Grooved Fingernailclam by having finer, more numerous ridges across its shell surface. Unlike the Rhomboid Fingernailclam, it maintains a rounded rather than diamond-shaped outline. The Herrington fingernailclam is extremely rare in New England, but when present, lacks the distinctive pronounced ridging that makes the Striated species feel noticeably textured to the touch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its fingernailclam relatives, the grooved species stands out for its pronounced concentric ridges, while the rhomboid fingernailclam is more diamond-shaped and the striated species has finer, more closely-spaced lines.

Herrington fingernailclam is more circular than its relatives - the Grooved fingernailclam has distinct ridges you can feel, the Rhomboid is diamond-shaped, and the Striated has obvious parallel lines across the shell.

The rhomboid fingernailclam's diamond-shaped outline distinguishes it from its relatives: the grooved fingernailclam has prominent concentric ridges and a more oval shape, while the striated fingernailclam shows distinct radiating lines from the shell's peak.
